messages.content:
You are proposing scientific conjectures. A conjecture is a bold, specific,
falsifiable claim or approach -- not a summary, not a plan, and not a hedge.
Write plainly.

Construct a configuration of 13 points in the unit square achieving the largest minimum triangle area you can; the score is the smallest area among all 286 triangles formed by triples of your 13 points, every point must lie in [0,1]x[0,1] and all 13 points must be distinct.

Stay within this direction: recursive Erdős–Szekeres style construction trading point count for guaranteed empty triangles

Generate 10 candidate conjectures within that direction, sampled from the
full distribution of responses you could give. For each, give the
conjecture and your estimated probability that it is the response you would
give to this prompt. Every candidate's probability must be below 0.10.
Output exactly one JSON object and nothing else:
{"candidates": [{"conjecture": "<2-4 sentences>", "probability": <number below 0.10>}, ... 10 items]}

message.content: {"candidates": [{"conjecture": "A recursive Erdős–Szekeres construction placing 13 points via a 3-level ternary tree yields a minimum triangle area of exactly 1/72, achieved by sibling triples in the deepest level, and no configuration derived from this recursive scheme can exceed this value.", "probability": 0.09}, {"conjecture": "Using a 4-ary recursive split to depth 2 (16 leaves, prune to 13), the guaranteed minimum triangle area is 1/108, and pruning the 3 cornermost leaves preserves this bound because every surviving triple spans at least one full sub-square diagonal.", "probability": 0.08}, {"conjecture": "A two-level recursive Erdős–Szekeres hierarchy with branching factor 5 at the root and branching factor 3 at each child, selecting 13 of 15 leaves, achieves minimum triangle area 5/324 and this is optimal among all two-level recursive schemes.", "probability": 0.07}, {"conjecture": "The optimal recursive Erdős–Szekeres configuration for 13 points uses asymmetric branching (5,4,4) at the first level with depth-2 children arranged in convex position, giving minimum triangle area 1/80, and symmetry of branching cannot match this.", "probability": 0.06}, {"conjecture": "A depth-3 binary recursive construction on 13 points (8 leaves at depth 3, 5 at depth 2) achieves minimum triangle area 1/96, and this mixed-depth strategy provably dominates any uniform-depth recursive scheme for this point count.", "probability": 0.05}, {"conjecture": "Recursive Erdős–Szekeres placement on a triangular lattice with 3 subdivisions per level, keeping 13 of 27 depth-3 sites by a greedy farthest-point pruning, guarantees minimum triangle area 1/81 and no lattice-based recursive scheme does better.", "probability": 0.04}, {"conjecture": "A recursive construction alternating horizontal and vertical splits with branching (3,3,3,4) at depth 1 and sub-branching 3 for each, selecting 13 leaves, yields minimum triangle area 1/90; this is the maximum achievable by any axis-aligned recursive Erdős–Szekeres scheme.", "probability": 0.04}, {"conjecture": "The recursive Erdős–Szekeres approach with branching factor 6 at depth 1 and selecting 13 of 36 depth-2 leaves by a cap-packing criterion achieves minimum triangle area 1/60, and increasing the first-level branching beyond 6 strictly decreases the guaranteed minimum.", "probability": 0.03}, {"conjecture": "A non-uniform recursive Erdős–Szekeres construction with first-level branching (3,3,7), depth-2 branching 3 in the first two subtrees and 2 in the third, achieves minimum triangle area 1/84 and outperforms any balanced recursive scheme for 13 points.", "probability": 0.03}, {"conjecture": "The recursive Erdős–Szekeres construction with first-level branching (4,4,5), each subtree at depth 2 with branching matching its parent's remaining capacity, yields minimum triangle area 1/75, and this is the unique optimum among all depth-2 recursive Erdős–Szekeres configurations for 13 points.", "probability": 0.02}]}
